newsitem.title: FRANCE: EP approves directive on food labels.
newsitem.headline: EP approves directive on food labels.

text.p: The European Parliament approved on Tuesday an agreement with the Council on a new European Union directive on labelling, advertising and presentation of foodstuffs.

The directive, COM(91)536, deadlocked for many months in conciliation negotiations before the two institutions reached a deal on October 17, is designed to provide consumers with more information about the products they are eating.
An update of Directive 79/112/EEC, it should also ensure the language used on labels is easier for customers to understand.

Parliament agreed to the final text only after winning an assurance from the European Commission on Monday that it would come forward with a separate proposal on labelling alcoholic drinks, which are not covered by the directive.
Novel foods, such as genetically modified tomatoes, are not covered either and are the subject of a separate Commission proposal.

The directive approved by Parliament on Tuesday will oblige foodstuff labels to give more information on the sales name of products, their composition and ingredients, and indicate whether they contain starches likely to contain gluten.
Information about starches is important for people who are allergic to gluten.

Under the compromise between Council and Parliament, member states may insist that labels carry "descriptive information" as well as the product's sales name but they cannot oblige manufacturers to include information about a product's content in the sales name itself.

This follows a decision by the European Court of Justice in October to rule against a German demand that imports of bearnaise sauce not made with butter in the traditional German way be labelled "bearnaise sauce made with vegetable oil".

The compromise text exempts manufacturers from indicating the quantity of an ingredient which appears in a product's name when this does not serve to distinguish the foodstuff from a similar product and has no influence on the consumer's choice.
Thus they will not have to detail the amount of malt in their "malt whisky" but will have to say how much salami is in their "salami pizzas".
Member states will have to ban the sale of products which do not conform to the new rules three years after the directive comes into force.
But goods labelled before that date can still be sold until the stocks run out.
The directive now goes to the Council for final approval.
